I have often found that the content of India 360 is accentuated by a sense of over-righteousness. As I tuned in to CNN-IBN on Monday evening, I realised that continuity makes me comfortable. Moderated by Sagarika Ghosh, that eternal tobacco debate enraged the usual panelists. Ever so often, you heard the word 'Children' being dropped. The word, I am convinced, is perhaps the last and only effective weapon left in the anti-smoking lobby's arsenal.
The argument is simple—film and TV personalities should not be seen with a stick of nicotine dangling from their lips because they are role models whom our infants are just waiting to emulate. The 'cool' factor forces me to concede some credence to that point of view, but the proposition that all sales of tobacco should be banned because the country's future will blow itself out through the proverbial chimney has left me baffled. Any sane adult is aware of the risks that come with cigarettes, but if he chooses to challenge fate, that surely should be an option given to him or her, on or off screen. If the impressionable child still buys himself a pack, the buck needs to stop with the parents.
I mull over this point because the debate is symptomatic of a larger sanitised utopia, imagined repetitively by the right. Cable operators in Bombay are refused permission to broadcast because some of the movie channels aired films that disregarded the 'A' certificate.
